newsitem.title: Bosnia: Refugee return problems gnaw at Bosnian peace.
newsitem.headline: Refugee return problems gnaw at Bosnian peace.

text.p: Unemployed Moslem men loiter in the streets and cafes of this former frontline town all day, brooding on how and when they will return to homes from which they were driven during the Bosnian war.

"We spend our days as you see us, standing, walking, talking -- but always wondering how we will get home and who will help us," said Fered Kucalovic, 38, a refugee from Koraj, just nine km (six miles) east of Celic.
"I left Koraj in 1992 and spent the whole war on the frontline in Celic because I didn't want to go far from my house. I am fed up with waiting. I want to go home even if it means fighting again."

The Bosnian war ended, on paper at least, with the signing of the Dayton Peace accord a year ago. Among other things, the agreement said that several million Bosnian refugees would have the right to return to their homes.

In fact, U.N. refugee officials say no more than 250,000 people have gone home in Bosnia over the past year and that virtually none of them have been able to cross de facto ethnic borders which divide the country's Moslems, Croats and Serbs.

While none of the former warring factions is anxious to host returning refugees from rival ethnic communities, the U.N. refugee agency singles out Bosnian Serbs, who control 49 percent of the country, as the worst offenders.

The international community has patched together an application process for refugee returns in what is known as the Zone of Separation (ZOS) -- a 1,000-km (600-mile) long strip of former frontline territory patrolled by NATO-led peace forces.
But even in the ZOS only a few hundred homes have been re- occupied and those with difficulty and some bloodshed.

Two Moslems were killed and a number of Moslems and Serbs were injured this week when Moslem refugees, who had not received approval to return to their homes, crossed into Serb territory and set up a squatter camp in the village of Gajevi, between Celic and Koraj.
NATO blamed the Bosnian government for provoking the incident by orchestrating the unapproved return.
Moslems from Gajevi say their applications had been under consideration for more than the three weeks.
On Wednesday Fadil Banjanovic, a fiery Bosnian government refugee coordinator, paced his office in Celic like a caged panther, excoriating the international community.
"When we were being driven from our homes and killed like dogs during the war where was the international community with its forms and its applications?" he added.

"Where in the Dayton peace accord does it say that I must apply for permission to return to my own home? It would be more honourable if the international mediators who make these rules would resign from their jobs rather than play this silly game."

The running skirmishes which broke out between Moslems and Croats around Gajevi may have been the worst violence to hit Bosnia since Serbs wrecked Sarajevo suburbs as they abandoned them in early 1996.
NATO officers worry the problem of refugee returns may get worse if, as expected, significant numbers of refugees living in Eupean countries are forced to return to Bosnia in 1997.

"There are no significant returns of ethnic minorities to majority areas. The serbs did not fight a war for ethnic purity so they could hand over their half of Bosnia to Moslems and Croats," said a NATO officer who asked not to be named.

"This is a political problem and it requires urgent attention by Bosnian leaders and by the international community. Otherwise we are going to find NATO forces sitting on a hornet's nest, which is what happened in Gajevi."
Samir, 26, an engineer from Tuzla, says the refugee return issue could undermine the entire Dayton peace agreement.
"Look at these men from Koraj in Celic. They are young. They fought the war and survived. They want to work and raise families, they want what is theirs," he said.

"And yet here they are living in someone else's house, no job, begging cigarettes from a strangers. For them fighting to go home would not be the worst thing. It would be better than what they have now."
